Viviane, right? We met at the panel. I run HR for the group across the street.
Hello, Nick. I know your company. Your bonus is bigger than ours.
It is. And still, three of my store managers went to you last year. Why?
Because we are more flexible than you are. And our career path is clearer — we published it.
Is your turnover really lower, or is that a marketing number?
Sorry, could you repeat the question?
Your turnover. Is it really lower than the sector, or is it a nice number for the report?
It is real. Eleven points lower. But you pay better than we do, and I am not going to pretend that is not true.
That is the most honest answer I have heard today. Send me that benchmark, I will send you mine.
Our turnover is eleven points lower than the sector average.
Our salary is as competitive as theirs.
Our reputation is stronger than it was two years ago.

Last year I had two offers on the table and I chose the smaller company. Everybody told me I was wrong. The other one was bigger, the salary was about fifteen per cent higher, and the office was nicer. So why did I say no? Three reasons. First, the manager. In the second interview the manager of the smaller company asked me better questions. She wanted to know what I was bad at. Nobody asks that. Second, the career path was clearer. They showed me a real document, with real steps, and the bigger company only said we will see in a year. And third, the commute is shorter, which sounds small until you add it up. Forty minutes a day, every day. Money is easier to compare than everything else, so people compare the money and forget the rest. I did the opposite, and one year later I am still happy.

There is one question that comes up in every process, on both sides of the table. Why you and not them. When I am hiring, the candidate asks me. When I am the candidate, they ask me. And the worst answer is always the same: the one where everything is perfect. We are more flexible, we pay better, we grow faster, our culture is stronger. Nobody believes it, because no company is better at everything. The answer that works has three parts. One thing where you are clearly better, with a number if you have one. One thing where you are honestly worse. And then the sentence that ties it together: so if what matters most to you is money, they are the better choice, and if it is stability, we are. That last sentence sounds like you are losing the argument. You are not. You are the only person in the room who sounds true.

We are more flexible than most retail companies. Our career path is clearer, because we published it. Our store turnover is eleven points lower than the sector average. Their bonus is bigger than ours, and that is true.
